coherence.reasons: Both run the same clean chain: growth is real, orders lose money, the pop-up is weaker still, the plan breaks the runway, so fund software. Y's hierarchy is tighter: each summary point maps to one slide whose title states the finding, and the Zipcart counter-evidence sits in its own slide feeding a reopening trigger. X is also well structured around five sub-questions, but raises a heavily assumption-laden estimate to summary level ("buying density would cost more than the cash", the $13.7M acquisition figure). Y has one loose title: "at best break even" relies on an unobserved cut of promotions to 2%.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (decline, fund software, sell store-based fast delivery, set re-entry tests). X goes further in testing its own recommendation against the board's objectives: it models software break-even at about $11M ARR, shows cash through 2028, and admits the path fails the runway floor if growth drops to 30%. It also lists the risks of saying no with owners and signals. Y simply asserts the runway rule is "kept" on the software path. Y's reopening triggers are better designed, since they include a service-fee test and rider-pay clarity, and it adds the customer-conflict and focus trade-off. On balance X weighs the trade-offs of the recommended alternative more fully.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core figures right: -$6.17, -$1.76, -$12.57, $2.5M and about 6 months, and -$1.05 for Zipcart's levers at the median. Y's numbers all check, including the 42% CAGR, the +$0.22 to +$1.52 range for missing one target, the nine-store totals and +$3.97 for Zipcart's levers at best observed inputs. Y also makes the sharp inference that the 14 benchmark sites already run Parcelbird software, so the claimed software edge is already in the numbers. X adds valid extras (break-even AOV $63.4, 14.4 orders per rider-hour, -$0.48 with no volume loss) but leans on shakier extrapolations: the $13.7M acquisition bill, the 15-month payback and a software cash model with an unexplained "25 months of runway". Its claim that the plan loses about $0.30 without the order-value lever is path-dependent; the true figure is about -$0.73. X never states the CAGR. Y's one loose claim is calling store cost the biggest line separating loss from break-even.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while conceding that market growth is real, and both avoid the traps on promotion-fuelled growth and survey intent. Y handles the partly supportive Zipcart evidence more fairly. It shows the fee and promotion levers still lose about $1 at the median but turn positive at best observed inputs, calls pricing "the only lever with evidence behind it", notes the founders' plan includes no fee, and builds a fee test into the reopening triggers. X shows only that the fix fails at the median (-$0.48 and -$1.05) and frames it as a mere price rise, without acknowledging that it works at high density. Y also gives an explicit fair caveat on the pop-up's immaturity; X notes it more briefly.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, defensible answers with correct core calculations and the same recommendation. Y serves the board slightly better: its arithmetic is error-free, it rebuts the founders' software-edge claim directly, it treats the Zipcart evidence in a balanced way, and it ends with crisp decisions and triggers tied to the evidence. X's advantage is its stress test of the software path against the profitability and runway objectives and its risk register for saying no. That is offset by several assumption-heavy extrapolations given headline weight and a one-sided reading of Zipcart.
